title: Sainz on bringing F1 back to his home city of Madrid
excerpt:
Carlos Sainz knows what it's like to have a home Grand Prix, the Spaniard having competed in 12 of them in Formula 1 in Barcelona. He knows how to deliver for his home fans, too, having scored in each of the first 10 of those appearances. But never has he raced in a Formula 1 Grand Prix in his home city of Madrid – until now.

This weekend, he'll compete in the Spanish Grand Prix in Madrid, on a new part-street, part-purpose-built 22-turn circuit called the Madring. The 32-year-old has played a key role in the project from acting as an adviser to helping promote it. The passion he has for the event is infectious.

"I've been lucky enough to have a home race pretty much all through my career thanks to the Grand Prix in Barcelona," says Sainz when we chat all things Madrid in the Williams hospitality unit. "The fact that it's a lot closer to my [family] home, only 15 minutes by car, and all my family and all my friends are from there, it's probably going to feel even more special.

title: 8 of the best debut Grands Prix in F1 history
excerpt:
F1 is heading to Madrid to race at a brand-new track this coming weekend, with the hugely exciting Madring set to make its bow as part of the 2026 season.

The drivers will have to contend with looming walls, some extreme banking and hot temperatures in Spain, meaning the world of F1 could be in for a very exciting weekend.

But while we patiently wait to see the cars hit the Madring later this week, let’s take a look at the sort of racing other tracks threw up in their inaugural Grand Prix.

From Championship fights to crashes, mechanical failures to team mate disputes, a few tracks certainly had debuts to remember…

Las Vegas 2023 – Glitz, glamour and plenty of drama

While Las Vegas had previously hosted the Caesars Palace Grand Prix, the Las Vegas Strip Circuit joined the calendar in 2023 for a spectacular night race against the backdrop of many iconic locations.

Ferrari initially locked out the front row in Qualifying, only for Carlos Sainz to be penalised for needing new PU parts. That left Charles Leclerc on pole and Max Verstappen second, those two delighting fans with wheel-to-wheel racing around the opening lap.

Leclerc emerged in the lead, Verstappen penalised for forcing his rival wide as the City of Lights was treated to some early drama. Sergio Perez also got involved in the battle up front, while Safety Cars meant the front runners diverged on strategy.

George Russell and Verstappen clashed at one point, Lando Norris crashed out and Fernando Alonso spun in a race where grip was at a premium in the cooler night time conditions.

In the end, Verstappen took the win courtesy of a great move on Leclerc, who managed to hold onto second despite Perez briefly also getting past. And as if the racing was not enough, Verstappen then got to pick up his trophy in front of the famous Bellagio fountains to boot.

Miami 2022 – Verstappen wins in the Sunshine State

Miami joined the calendar in 2022, the first year with a new generation of cars. The new track proved a hit too, the picturesque circuit winding its way around the Hard Rock Stadium complex in Miami Gardens.

Red Bull got out of the gates fast in 2022, with Verstappen the favourite to defend his title. The Dutchman won the first race in Miami, but was made to work exceptionally hard for victory with Leclerc hot on his heels for much of the Grand Prix.

Verstappen actually started third, but picked off Sainz and Leclerc to move into the lead and initially seemed like he would be untroubled from there. But then came a Pierre Gasly/Norris crash, which ripped the wheel off the McLaren and caused a Safety Car.

Some of the field came in for fresh tyres, others stayed out, and when the race resumed Verstappen could not get his hard tyres back up to temperature. He was forced to absorb plenty of pressure from Leclerc, with a freshly shod Perez also making moves from behind.

But the Dutchman just about hung on for the win, and did indeed go on to defend his title in 2022.

Saudi Arabia 2021 – Title rivals go head-to-head

When Saudi Arabia’s Jeddah Corniche Circuit arrived on the calendar in 2021, anticipation was high for a track that boasted some incredible speeds, with conditions set to be incredibly testing for the whole field.

The drama in Jeddah started on Saturday, when Verstappen crashed in Qualifying and lost his chance to start on pole. That left rival Lewis Hamilton to take the top spot, and he initially led from pole at the start of the race.

Madring shares new photos ahead of Madrid's maiden GP

But the drama never let up on Sunday, with two pivotal red flag stoppages shaking things up. After the first, Verstappen went wide and cut back onto the track ahead of Hamilton, who also lost out to Esteban Ocon – before two crashes behind halted proceedings once again.

The next restart saw Ocon start ahead of Hamilton with Verstappen third, before the Dutchman took the lead when the others tangled. That was not enough drama though, with three VSC periods shaking things up once again. Before the chequered flag fell, there was also contact between Verstappen and Hamilton, the former told to cede position but doing so in such a place that the latter was caught unawares and he hit the rear wing of the Red Bull.

And for final measure, the two went side by side again, Verstappen running wide to retain the lead and in the end the stewards got involved. It proved a reasonably bad tempered affair, but crucially saw Hamilton draw level on points with his rival…

Portimao 2020 – A new venue in an unusual season

Portugal had hosted F1 races before, but in 2020, Portimao answered the call as the sport managed to return to racing amidst the Covid-19 pandemic. The Algarve International Circuit is set to return again next season, which based on past results bodes very well for the sport.

In 2020, Hamilton was putting together a dominant season for Mercedes. He recorded his 92nd Grand Prix victory at the circuit, to break Michael Schumacher’s long-standing record for most race wins.

That was not the only thing Portimao was remembered for, with differing strategies in play causing plenty of overtakes in the early stages.

Sainz wound up leading from seventh on the grid after the opening exchanges, before Mercedes were able to recover – leading to an intra-team fight between Hamilton and Valtteri Bottas, with the former taking one of the 11 victories he amassed across the season.

Azerbaijan 2016 – Rosberg takes the win on his title charge

The 2016 season will always be remembered for the fight at Mercedes between title holder Hamilton and team mate Nico Rosberg. It was the latter who took the inaugural win in Baku, at what was then named the European Grand Prix.

Rosberg was relatively untroubled around the unique city circuit, which has long wide straights, right-angled corners and then the tight and twisty castle section. But behind there was trouble brewing for his team mate.

Hamilton was struggling with reliability woes, climbing to fourth from a P10 grid slot before falling back with an ERS issue. That loss of points was one of many moments across the season he can point to as to where the title got away.

But while there was little joy for Hamilton, there was plenty for the fans with an action-packed race stuffed full of overtakes, with Baku delivering the goods – something it has continued to do ever since.

Turkey 2005 – Raikkonen makes late bid to stop Alonso’s charge

When Turkey joined the world of F1 in 2005, there was a clash of eras going on, with Fernando Alonso putting together a championship charge as Michael Schumacher’s dominance began to fade. But there was a third driver in play, with Kimi Raikkonen trying to haul a slower-starting McLaren to the title.

Raikkonen started on pole at Istanbul Park, the circuit immediately proving popular with drivers and fans alike. The Finn wound up taking the victory, but it was what was going on behind that added plenty of spice to proceedings.

Juan Pablo Montoya was running second, but collided with a back marker late on which allowed Alonso through to take P2, and some crucial extra championship points. Meanwhile, Schumacher and Mark Webber had a coming together too, in a race filled with incidents.

Despite a late run of victories, neither McLaren driver could overhaul Alonso who went on to take his maiden championship title in 2005.

Malaysia 1999 – A comeback race in attritional conditions

Malaysia joined the calendar in 1999 and was remembered as Schumacher’s comeback race, the German having sustained a broken leg in Silverstone earlier in the season. But it was also notable for how hard it was on drivers and cars, with just 11 finishers seeing the chequered flag.

There was some Ferrari shenanigans in play in Sepang, with a dominant Schumacher dropping behind Eddie Irvine to try and back the pack up, aiding his team mate’s title chances. Somehow Schumacher did manage to keep everyone at bay, with the Scuderia scoring a 1-2.

The drama did not stop when the track action ended though, with both scarlet cars disqualified for a technical breach, only to be reinstated on appeal.

So, all in all, Malaysia certainly delivered a first race to remember.

Hungary 1986 – One of the great overtakes

While Hungary had hosted a race back in the thirties, the Hungaroring joined the calendar in what was a historic first race behind the Iron Curtain in 1986. The track is often compared to a go-kart ring and it is easy to see why, with a series of sweeping corners and very few straights.

But the inaugural Grand Prix will always be remembered for one of the great overtaking moments in F1 history. Nelson Piquet dived around the outside of Ayrton Senna’s Lotus into Turn 1 and he managed to just hold his Williams ahead as he got sideways through the corner – the two just avoiding contact.

Piquet went on to win the race from Senna and team mate Nigel Mansell, who in third finished a lap down in a Grand Prix where 16 cars did not make it to the flag.

title: What is the weather forecast for the Spanish Grand Prix?
excerpt:
The 2026 Formula 1 season continues this weekend with the Spanish Grand Prix, taking place at the newly-built Madring in the nation's capital – but what kind of weather conditions are in store for the drivers and teams?

title: What tyres will the teams have for the Spanish Grand Prix?
excerpt:
The Madring will make its debut on the Formula 1 calendar when it hosts Round 14, the Spanish Grand Prix – and tyre suppliers Pirelli have confirmed the compounds that will be in use throughout the weekend.

Pirelli will provide the drivers and teams with their C2 (as the hard), C3 (as the medium) and C4 (as the soft) compounds at the brand-new track, with tyre management likely to be a big talking point due to the smooth surface.

Drivers will get two sets of the hard tyre (marked white), three sets of the medium tyre (marked yellow), and eight sets of the soft tyre (marked red), as well as access to the green intermediate tyre and the blue full wets, should they be required.

An extra set of softs is reserved for those who reach Q3 in Qualifying, while all drivers must use at least two different slick compounds during the race, providing the track is dry.

"The start-finish line and Turn 1 are separated by just 200 metres," reads Pirelli's weekend preview. "The first sector is very fast and leads into a second section featuring several medium and low-speed corners, including the banked Turn 12. The final part of the lap also includes a number of 90-degree corners similar to those drivers encounter in Baku.

"Pirelli's work to identify the forces that tyres will be subjected to at the Madring began three years ago, when the designers provided the first information on the final layout. Using simulation tools, the trajectories that the cars would follow around the circuit were identified and, consequently, the loads to which the tyres would be exposed were calculated.

"Once the circuit had been completed, a group of Pirelli engineers visited the venue to measure the asphalt's macro and micro roughness, refine the simulations and produce a technical briefing document that was shared with the teams to support their preparation for this new event.

"From an energy perspective, the Madrid circuit ranks among the five most demanding on the calendar, with lateral forces comparable in intensity to those recorded at Barcelona and Silverstone. The "Monumental" is the corner that generates the highest vertical load of the season, not only because of its banking but also because of its length.

"Its configuration will also present a significant challenge in terms of tyre grip. Drivers may adopt different approaches when tackling it, depending on how much they wish to prioritise the opportunity to attack into the following corner.

"The asphalt is very smooth and therefore offers a relatively low level of grip. For this reason, it has been treated with high-pressure water jets, as is already done at other circuits, including Singapore, to remove dust and oily residues typically associated with newly laid surfaces."

title: Kimi Raikkonen's son joins Red Bull Junior Team
excerpt:
Red Bull have announced the signing of Robin Raikkonen, son of 2007 World Champion Kimi Raikkonen, to their driver development programme.

The 11-year-old, who is also known by the nickname 'Ace', will officially start working with the team from 2027 onwards to further his racing career.

Red Bull have proven over the years that they have one of the strongest junior programmes in Formula 1, with their graduates including Max Verstappen, Carlos Sainz and this season's sole rookie Arvid Lindblad.

Identified as "one of the most promising young talents of his generation", the young Raikkonen has already demonstrated his skill in various karting championships and will be supported through the ranks.

Former Ferrari racer Raikkonen said: "We are all thrilled and excited that Robin has been chosen to further his racing path as a member of the Red Bull Junior Team. Laurent [Mekies] and everyone else at Red Bull have been incredibly supportive throughout all our discussions.

"They offer a compelling and comprehensive programme to develop and nurture Robin’s progress over the coming years and provide him with all the experience required to develop his natural talent, which has amply been displayed in all his karting endeavours to date.

"Red Bull’s Junior Team has had years of incredible success. Its alumni include Sebastian Vettel and Verstappen amongst many others. It is thus with great humility that Robin joins this illustrious programme, and he will dedicate all his efforts to warrant the trust that Red Bull is placing in him.”

"Robin has already demonstrated exceptional ability in karting," added Red Bull Team Principal Mekies. "His speed, racecraft and natural talent have established him as one of the most promising young drivers in his age group. At the same time, he impresses with his maturity, his calm approach and his clear focus on driving.

"Our goal is to develop him step by step, without placing any unnecessary pressure on his shoulders. The path through motorsport is a long one, and we will give him the time, support and resources he needs to maximise his potential.

"We strongly believe that talent can thrive when supported by the right people, the right culture and the right environment. That is what we are committed to providing Robin as he continues his development. We are very much looking forward to taking the next steps in his journey together with Robin and his family."

title: Williams reveal special livery ahead of Spanish GP in Madrid
excerpt:
Williams will mark Formula 1's return to Madrid by racing a special edition livery inspired by the colours of their 1981 championship-winning FW07C, which was the car the team raced the last time the sport competed in the Spanish capital.

The livery, which will adorn the cars of home hero Carlos Sainz and his team mate Alex Albon, features a white, green and navy blue colourway in a nod to the 1981-design that was raced by Alan Jones and Carlos Reutemann at Madrid's Circuito de Jarama.

Williams say the design showcases how they are using the knowledge, methods and lessons of the past to inspire their fight back to the front.

"From the engineers who developed the FW07C to the team mates preparing the FW48, the same spirit of innovation, precision and teamwork continues to shape Williams," said the British team.

The one-off design was revealed during a Fan Zone appearance with Sainz in Madrid's Plaza De Callao on Tuesday evening, ahead of the first Spanish Grand Prix on the new part-street, part-purpose-built 22-turn Madring.

“Our mission to get back to the front of the grid is drawn from, inspired by and informed by everything we’ve done before," said Team Principal James Vowles.

"I am incredibly proud to celebrate that through [title sponsor] Atlassian’s special livery, connecting the team we were at Jarama with the team we are becoming today through focused collaboration, improved technological innovation, and real creativity.

"The car looks fantastic, and I cannot wait to see it lapping around Madrid.”

Sainz will be competing in his 13th Spanish Grand Prix but first in Madrid - the city where he was born, raised and began his motor racing career.

He and team mate Alex Albon will be searching for the team's first points since Albon took eighth in Monaco, eight Grand Prix weekends ago.

The British team, who finished a superb fifth last year, currently sit ninth in the Teams' Championship on 11 points, five adrift of Audi.

title: Max Verstappen outlines greatest desire for post-F1 career
excerpt:
Max Verstappen has set his sights on taking part in endurance racing once he opts to bring his F1 career to an end.

The four-time champion has long voiced his appreciation for endurance competition and often takes part in virtual events on his simulator.

He also dipped his toes into the world earlier this year with an appearance at the 24 Hours of Nurburgring, having had several outings at the Nordschleife in preparation for the event.

Verstappen recently extended his Red Bull contract until the end of 2030 as he targets a return to the front of the field with the Milton Keynes-based squad.

But having already had a taste of endurance racing, Verstappen insisted that he is only getting started.

When asked what else is on his bucket list, Verstappen told BBC Sport: "All the endurance races.

“Eventually, of course also Hypercar [the world endurance championship]. I don't want to rush it.

“I want to do it in the right environment. On my terms. And competitive."

In the past, it has been suggested that Verstappen and Fernando Alonso could team up for an entry at the 24 Hours of Le Mans - the most prestigious endurance race.

Verstappen has confirmed he has discussed the possibility with his fellow champion, but admitted scheduling conflicts could get in the way.

"We've talked about it. I mean, look at Fernando,” Verstappen said.

“He's 45 and he's still flying. Especially for Le Mans, with his experience, it could be a good option. It needs to fit our schedules.

“It needs to make sense. It needs to be on my terms. And there needs to be a real chance to go there and win it."

title: F1 driver remains conscious after 'violent' airborne crash - On This Day
excerpt:
On this day 36 years ago, former F1 driver Derek Warwick suffered a terrifying accident in Monza yet managed to restart the race!

On 9 September 1990, Ayrton Senna delivered a masterclass at Monza with a grand slam victory in the Italian Grand Prix. But it was Derek Warwick's extraordinary accident at the Parabolica that remains seared into the memory of everyone who witnessed it.

Warwick, driving the Lotus 102 for Camel Team Lotus, was following Mauricio Gugelmin's car closely at the end of the opening lap when he got caught in the aerodynamic turbulence.

At speeds estimated around 150 mph, the Lotus understeered wide, clipped the grass on the exit of the Parabolica, and struck the barrier with tremendous force.

The impact launched the car into a barrel roll, sending it sliding upside down across the track as debris scattered in all directions. Marshals had to dive clear.

A brief fire broke out before extinguishing itself as the destroyed Lotus came to rest, its survival cell mercifully intact.

Warwick, remarkably, was conscious throughout. He later explained his composure in chillingly matter-of-fact terms: "I was conscious all the time... My first reaction after that was 'I'm okay' and my second was, 'spare car.'"

He climbed out unaided, ran back to the pits, and, after medical checks declared him fit, jumped into the spare Lotus for the restart. His race ultimately ended with a clutch failure, but his survival was the real story.

Senna victory overshadowed

The severity of Warwick's crash triggered an immediate red flag at the end of lap one, with the race restarted over its full 53-lap distance. From there, Senna controlled proceedings from pole to chequered flag, also setting the fastest lap to complete a grand slam for McLaren-Honda.

Alain Prost brought his Ferrari home second, 6.054 seconds adrift, with Gerhard Berger completing the podium in the second McLaren.

Nigel Mansell finished fourth in the other Ferrari, while both Benetton drivers lost time through troublesome pit stops, with the leading cars all running non-stop strategies.

It was Senna's 26th career victory, but the image that endured from that afternoon at Monza was not one of triumph. It was a Lotus sliding on its back through the Parabolica, a driver walking away from wreckage that looked entirely unsurvivable, and then asking for the spare car.

"It was a violent impact but I'm OK, no problem!" Warwick told reporters with characteristic nonchalance. Thirty-six years on, it remains one of the most spectacular survivable accidents the sport has ever seen.

title: 2026 F1 Spanish Grand Prix - Madrid weather forecast
excerpt:
F1 heads to Madrid this weekend for the inaugural Spanish Grand Prix at the brand-new Circuito de Madring, a 5.416km, 22-corner hybrid layout winding around the IFEMA exhibition centre and through the Valdebebas district.

The circuit blends tight, street-style corners in its southern section with faster, flowing sequences to the north, headlined by the spectacular 24%-banked "La Monumental" corner.

It replaces the Circuit de Barcelona-Catalunya, which hosted the race since 1991.

As for the conditions greeting drivers on this historic weekend, the paddock should brace itself.

There is no rain expected across any of the three days, but the heat will be relentless.

Friday's opening practice sessions are forecast to see temperatures climb to around 30°C, with a very light southerly breeze offering little in the way of relief.

That warmth will only intensify as the weekend progresses, with Saturday's forecast predicting 31°C during the late afternoon, precisely when qualifying is scheduled.

Managing tyre warm-up could prove tricky in those conditions, as the extreme track surface temperatures may push rubber beyond its optimal operating window before drivers can extract a clean lap.

Sunday, however, looks set to be the most punishing day of all, with 33°C forecast for race day. At that level, it is very likely the FIA will formally declare a Heat Hazard.

Under the current Sporting Regulations, the Race Director initiates the protocol when the official weather forecast predicts a heat index greater than 31.0°C at any point during the grand prix.

Once declared, teams are required to install driver cooling systems in the car, with health monitoring procedures also activated throughout the event.

title: Mercedes boss mindset explored after 'so difficult' team orders decision
excerpt:
Former Formula 1 driver David Coulthard has explored the mindset of Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff, who made the "so difficult" decision to let his drivers race in Monza.

Kimi Antonelli recovered from 19th on the grid to lead home another Mercedes one-two in the Italian Grand Prix, with the youngster taking the lead with three laps remaining.

Not for the first time this season, Antonelli and Russell battled hard across large portions of the race, with the championship leader at one stage going off the circuit.

A call did come to both drivers mid-race to hold position in an attempt to break away from Max Verstappen, which did lead to a brief moment of calm on circuit.

However, that went out of the window in the final laps, when the pair went to battle again for the Monza win. It was a situation where Wolff could have easily instructed the duo not to fight, yet no call came from the Austrian.

Coulthard praised the decision and the pure racer in the Mercedes boss, although he conceded that it must have been an extremely challenging choice to make.

Discussing Wolff not introducing team orders, Coulthard said on the Up to Speed podcast: "It was interesting, but to try and understand how close he was to sort of pushing the radio button to say, 'Right, guys, you know, we just need good points here. Of course, we want to win, but we don't need you tripping over each other.'

"And there was a moment early in the race where they did sort of calm them down. But in the latter stages, when the race came back on, I was going to say, 'I'm proud of Toto,' but who the hell am I to be proud of him?

"But it must be so difficult to not push that button because if you put yourself there, you're a shareholder and the team principal, and you're going to have a one-two.

"Putting your commercial head on, it would be really difficult. Putting your racer's head on, you'd be like, 'Right, bring it. Let's create something for the ages.'"

title: Max Verstappen predicts 'big shunts' at Madrid F1 weekend
excerpt:
Max Verstappen has predicted that there will be some “big shunts” throughout the upcoming Spanish Grand Prix weekend.

The Circuito de Madring will host its first F1 race event in the coming days, becoming the newest track to join the schedule.

The street circuit will pose a high-speed challenge for the drivers as they bid to become the first to stand on the top step of the podium at the venue.

At a recent Formula 3 test from Madrid, 19 red flags were deployed across two days, 11 of which were for contact with the barriers.

It has created speculation that the track could be the scene of multiple collisions throughout the weekend.

When asked if he has driven the track on his home setup, Verstappen replied: “Yeah I did, we also have it on the F1 sim.

“It's going to be very difficult. It's not an easy track. If you do a few laps in a row, it's always hard to cross the line and say 'I nailed the lap'.

“It's very hard. It also has a tendency of creating some big shunts in some places.”

F1 has seen an increase in visits to street circuits in recent years, with Jeddah, Miami and Las Vegas among those that have been included in the calendar.

Verstappen has likened the Madrid track to Jeddah, which is known as one of the most challenging circuits on the schedule.

“It reminds me a little bit of Jeddah in a way, with fast corners and the walls being very close,” he added.

title: Is Lewis Hamilton's eighth F1 title dream dead this year?
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton's Italian Grand Prix was supposed to be a springboard. Instead, it turned into a weekend that may well have ended his championship challenge.

A lap-one clash with teammate Charles Leclerc at the first chicane sent Hamilton tumbling from fourth on the grid to the lower reaches of the midfield, and from there, the damage was done.

Leclerc squeezed him wide, forcing the seven-time world champion off track and into the gravel. One lap later, Leclerc himself was out of the race after a high-speed crash at the Parabolica, leaving Hamilton as Ferrari's sole representative but already buried in the pack.

A questionable strategy call, in which Ferrari opted not to pit Hamilton under a mid-race Virtual Safety Car, compounded the misery.

He was left exposed on the straights, unable to match the straight-line speed of those around him, and eventually crossed the line in sixth, some 24 seconds behind race winner Kimi Antonelli.

"A bit devastating," Hamilton said afterwards. "Tough one to swallow. Lost a lot of points and ultimately couldn't keep a Mercedes engine behind. They were just out and out quicker."

The deficit to championship leader Antonelli now stands at 76 points with likely nine races remaining. Mathematically, it is still possible, but Hamilton himself appeared resigned to the reality of the situation.

"It's never over until it's over," he conceded. "I don't know how many points it is now, but I'm sure it's 60, 70... with the pace that they have, it's a very, very difficult amount to close out."

title: Red Bull announce Kimi Raikkonen's son as latest junior signing
excerpt:
Red Bull has confirmed the signing of Robin Raikkonen, son of F1 champion Kimi, to its F1 junior programme.

RacingNews365 first revealed Raikkonen's signing to Red Bull last weekend during the Italian Grand Prix.

Raikkonen is still in the early stages of his racing career, competing in karting championships as he prepares for a step up to single-seater competition in the coming years.

He now looks set to do so with Red Bull, who has added the Finn to its famous junior squad.

"Robin has already demonstrated exceptional ability in karting,” Red Bull team boss Laurent Mekies said.

“His speed, racecraft and natural talent have established him as one of the most promising young drivers in his age group.

“At the same time, he impresses with his maturity, his calm approach and his clear focus on driving.

“Our goal is to develop him step by step, without placing any unnecessary pressure on his shoulders.

“The path through motorsport is a long one, and we will give him the time, support and resources he needs to maximise his potential.

“We strongly believe that talent can thrive when supported by the right people, the right culture and the right environment. That is what we are committed to providing Robin as he continues his development.

“We are very much looking forward to taking the next steps in his journey together with Robin and his family."

Red Bull has worked with many young drivers throughout its history in motorsport, with its biggest success stories from the programme being Sebastian Vettel and Max Verstappen.

title: Carlos Sainz addresses Madrid F1 concern after red flag chaos
excerpt:
Carlos Sainz has played down the disruption F1 sessions could endure at Madrid next weekend.

The Madring will make its F1 debut when it hosts round 14 of the 2026 season, taking over as the location of the Spanish Grand Prix.

The track has been under construction for several years and recently held an in-season Formula 3 test in anticipation of the maiden race event.

During the test, 19 red flags were deployed across two days, 11 of which were for contact with the barrier.

It has generated concern that it could mean chaos for F1 this weekend, with Sainz acknowledging that the track will be a major challenge.

“With the way they've put the barriers and the design of the track, it's going to be one of the biggest challenges in F1 recently,” he said.

“The track reminds me a lot of Jeddah, reminds me a lot of Baku, even reminds me a bit of Macau in some ways.

“So having that in F1 with 1,000 horsepower is going to be quite an interesting challenge.”

However, Sainz insisted that F1 is no stranger to dealing with the challenge of high-speed street tracks with close barriers.

As a result, he does not expect the weekend to to feature many chaotic incidents.

“Looking at the track and hearing of what happened in the F3 test, I think we are all expecting safety cars and red flags and yellow flags in quali.

“But it's been a fashion or a tendency of F1 to go to these kind of tracks like Jeddah or Baku that are closer to the city.

“They have more walls, and we haven't had any issues with it. The races actually seem to be going quite well at every place we've gone.

“It's that same similar trend that we're going towards.”

title: Sebastian Vettel addresses losing F1 youngest champion record to Kimi Antonelli
excerpt:
Sebastian Vettel says he would be "very happy" to lose his tag as the 'youngest F1 world champion' to runaway 2026 leader Kimi Antonelli.

Antonelli leads the points table by 66 points following his Italian GP success last time out, coming through from 19th on the grid to claim a historic victory, his seventh of the season.

With potential 10 races remaining, Antonelli holds a buffer of nearly three grands prix worth over George Russell, and a further buffer of seven wins to Russell's two in case countback is required to seperate the two.

Having just turned 20 years old, Antonelli is on course to shatter Vettel's record from 2010 by over three years, with the German, who was born on July 3rd, 1987, having won his first title on November 14th, 2010 - at the age of 23 years, 4 months, 11 days.

For Antonelli to beat that, the Italian, who was born on August 25th, 2006, must win the F1 title before Saturday, 5th January 2030.

If the 2026 season goes down to the final race, currently scheduled for December 6th in Abu Dhabi, but understood to be moving to Europe, Antonelli would be 20 years, 3 months, 12 days.

Addressing the prospect of losing the record he's held for 16 years, Vettel was sanguine about the possibility.

"No," Vettel told media, including RacingNews365, when asked if it would be bittersweet to lose his record to Antonelli.

"I'd be very happy for him. He's had an incredible year, and there's the old phrase that records are there to be broken.

"He still has a lot of years ahead of him to do so.

"I love the sport, so as a spectator, it's very exciting. I'd wish for the others to come back and be more in the mix, but I'm sort of independent and happy for them because I know how much work there is behind it to achieve it.

"And whoever will win will deserve it."

title: George Russell details F1 title approach after latest setback
excerpt:
George Russell has conceded it will be “exceptionally challenging” to overcome Kimi Antonelli's advantage in the drivers' championship this year.

As a result, the Briton insisted he is giving no thought to the title fight.

Russell entered the Italian Grand Prix last weekend with a strong opportunity to eat into Antonelli's lead as the local favourite took a grid penalty for a new engine.

However, Antonelli quickly worked his way through the pack and soon found himself in the fight for the lead against Russell, passing him in the closing stages on fresher tyres.

Antonelli's victory now puts him 66 points ahead of Russell, leading the latter to praise his team-mate.

“Definitely Kimi’s in control of it and he’s deserving to be in control of it,” Russell told media including RacingNews365.

“For me personally, I’m not even thinking about a fight or a comeback or anything.

“I’m just focused on taking it race by race and trying to maximise every single weekend.”

Antonelli has had the upper hand on Russell for much of the year and has consistently edged out the gap as he targets a maiden title.

Russell asserted his target going forward is simply to maximise race weekends, rather than focusing on the points difference.

“He’s performing incredibly well,” Russell added. “It’s going to be exceptionally challenging to overcome that gap.

“I’m just sort of accepting that it is what it is and I’m just going to enjoy it from here on in and try and win as many races as possible.”

title: Formula E reveal crucial agreement in major global partnership
excerpt:
Formula E CEO Jeff Dodds has confirmed that there are agreements in place for Disney+ to advertise Formula E, following last month's announcement that it will become the official global streaming partner of the championship.

It was announced in August that, as part of a multi-year agreement, Formula E will be available on Disney+ across 144 territories, including the UK and the USA.

As part of the deal, every practice session, qualifying session and race will be available live, as will preview and review shows, highlights, on-demand replays and behind-the-scenes content.

It is one of, if not the biggest and most significant partnerships in the history of the all-electric series, and one which, with the exciting arrival of Gen4, should result in a substantial increase in global viewership.

Crucially, Disney+ will also advertise the series, something Amazon Prime failed to do for Formula E's 'Driver' docuseries. While the docuseries, which ran for two seasons, was impressive, it was practically impossible to find on the streaming site.

Finding it was only possible by specifically searching for 'Driver', creating an unwanted barrier to attracting new fans. Based on the agreements in place with Disney+, the same should be avoided.

Dodds is more than aware that Formula E will not be front and centre all the time on the platform, especially with significant movie releases coming up for Disney, but he has expressed that the American company is invested in and eager to grow the series.

"So yes, there are agreements with Disney about how they'll promote the racing," Dodds told RacingNews365 during an interview. "The difference being [from Amazon], this is an early sport for Disney+, and they have a very strong vested interest in this being really successful for them.

"They're investing a lot of resources into this, so I think we're mutually aligned that as you move into a race weekend, it's going to have prominence. People are going to know there's a race going on, and they're going to be directed, navigated through the platform to find it.

"On the other hand, they have a lot of new releases, right? So they'll be releasing big Marvel releases and things like that. It would be naive to think we're always going to be the most important thing on that platform because they have a lot of really important things on that platform.

"But yeah, we've talked to them about the promotion of the race series being really important to us, and they've given us all the reassurances we need that they will absolutely land that for us."

title: F1 braced for 'most severe' test with high-stress La Monumental Madring corner
excerpt:
Pirelli's chief F1 tyre engineer believes the championship will face the "most severe turn" with the "critical" banking at the new La Monumental corner at the Spanish Grand Prix.

Turn 12 at the new Madring is a long banked right-hander corner, which whilst not as steep in gradient as the final corner at Zandvoort, is considerably longer and will be taken at higher speed.

La Monumental has around 13.5 degrees of bank, far lower than Zandvoort, or indeed AVUS in Germany, which had a remarkable 43 degrees of bank.

This will place more stress on the tyres owing to the lateral loads, with Pirelli bringing the C2-C3-C4 tyres to the new race in the Spanish capital.

Whilst it does have some real-life track data from Ferrari's demo outing earlier in the year and the FIA F3 test, which featured 19 red flags over two days, Simone Berra believes the F1 drivers will be limited by pure grip available and not limited by power around the "critical and severe" banking.

"We gathered a lot of information, we went there also to measure the track because obviously it's very important to characterise as well the tarmac, which is an important factor for the tyres," Berra told media, including RacingNews365.

"The tarmac is pretty smooth as usual for a new tarmac. I would say also the level of bitumen is quite high, as they have performed high-pressure water jet cleaning, and this is obviously helped a lot in removing this bitumen layer and increasing the grip level for the test that we had with F3, we expect the track to be in slightly worse condition because in the next weeks.

"Some dust will come down, and the grip level will reduce a little bit. But we expect to start the week in a very good condition in this sense. In terms of the circuit itself, obviously the turn with the banking is the most critical and most severe; it is probably the most severe turn in the championship.

"We need to gather the real data, let's say, but on paper and from simulations, it seems so because it's a very long turn, limited by grip, not by the power, so they will be on the limit.

"Zandvoort is not grip limited now; it's power limited, and also in terms of duration, it is less in terms of seconds.

"I guess that if we see the pure energy that the turn gives to the tyres, it's higher. We are speaking about 20-20 per cent higher energy compared to the reference of Zandvoort.

"They can also try to they can try different approaches to that turn, different race lines, so it's very demanding that turn. For the rest, the walls are pretty close. We had a lot of red flags during the test, and with a lot of interruptions, that could be another factor.

"It's considered a normal street circuit like Singapore, so I would not be surprised to have significant incidents, let's say, or interruptions during both practice and the race."

title: McLaren eye F1 victory return with three tracks highlighted
excerpt:
McLaren team principal Andrea Stella has named three F1 tracks at which McLaren could once again impose itself in the fight for victory.

The Woking-based squad was unable to be a significant factor at Monza last weekend, with Mercedes possessing the fastest package.

Kimi Antonelli and George Russell brought home a 1-2 finish, with the former winning after starting from 19th on the grid.

Lando Norris ended the race in fourth place after making a last-lap overtake on team-mate Oscar Piastri, but it was a largely mellow weekend for the team that won the two races prior to Monza.

However, Stella does not see McLaren's chances of success now over, insisting upcoming tracks will play into its hands.

“A good, sensible, realistic end of the year is an end of the year in which the final nine or 10 races, we will see are sessions in which we can be consistently fighting for victories and achieve some of these victories,” he said.

“I think our tracks will be more the likes of Malaysia, Austin, Brazil. Here we have some long corners that seem to express its potential well.

“We have some new upgrades that we will take to Baku, but we still think that tracks like Baku and Madrid, where you have to be very precise with the trajectory, short corners, maybe they don't play to the best of our car.”

However, Stella is expecting the car to be more competitive this weekend in Madrid compared to Monza.

“Yet we have to say that in Zandvoort and Hungary, we were in position to win races, and here, while we were not, we know that it's a special race,” he said.

“This drag will be less important in Madrid, there's a much higher density of corners. So we will definitely give it a go.

“But from a championship point of view, I think we have to remain very realistic, don't get conditioned by looking at the classification. Just focus on one race at a time.”

title: Kimi Antonelli historic Italian GP victory rated - by the driver who won from further back
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli's victory in the Italian Grand Prix was the first time a driver had won from 19th on the grid since the 1954 Indianapolis 500 - some 1,128 world championship races ago.

But remarkably, Antonelli and Bill Vukovich have been one-upped by one driver who won from 22nd on the grid.

That was John Watson in the 1983 United States West GP at Long Beach as he stormed from 22nd on the 23-car grid to enter the record books and assume a record, which, having stood for 44 years and 787 grands prix, is likely to stand the test of time.

Reflecting on Antonelli's incredible drive, his seventh win of the season, and one which opened up a 66-point lead in the drivers' championship over George Russell, Watson has evaluated the Italian's achievement - and labelled him as a "fundamentally racer" who possesses a "unique" ability.

"There are some drivers who are what I would call fundamentally racers, and the people mentioned [above] were people that I would describe as racers,” Watson told Motor Sport.

"There are many fine racing drivers who have won grands prix and have been world champions, who have not, in my view, been what I would describe as an out-and-out racer.”

"It’s having this ability to make judgments when you’re catching a car. You must catch it in the right part of the racetrack to enable you to continue that progress, not to find yourself being bogged down and then losing your momentum.

"It comes down to a variety of qualities in the personality of the person and their ability behind the wheel to make those assessments and judgments. Execution is key ultimately, and you’ve got to be decisive.

"What he is doing presently is remarkable. George Russell, I’ve got a great respect for. I think he’s a bloody quick guy, and Kimi’s really overshadowing him, totally.

"Everybody felt it was George’s race to lose, and as it turns out, he did, and it was to his own team-mate.

"Antonelli has got something which is currently, I would say, unique amongst the entire Formula 1 field: a kid who’s just turned 20 with that maturity, along with that ability.

"It was a stellar drive, a world champion’s drive, and something that I think that he will be satisfied with, and quite rightly so as well."
